entries.term: a hell of a, one hell of a, one heck of a
entries.ipa: /ə ˈhɛl əv ə/, /ˌwʌn ˈhɛl əv ə/, /ˌwʌn ˈhɛk əv ə/
entries.respell: uh HELL uv uh, wun HELL uv uh, wun HECK uv uh — weak forms carry the whole phrase: of drops to /əv/ and then to /ə/, both articles are /ə/ (or /ən/ before a vowel), and the run-together result is the eye-spelling helluva /ˈhɛləvə/, HELL-uh-vuh. One is the exception: it resists reduction because it carries the emphasis, so it stays /wʌn/ and never becomes ✗ /wən/
entries.register: informal and spoken; hell is mildly profane, heck is the broadcast-safe swap, and helluva is a spelling of the sound rather than a word for edited prose
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only, because the frame ends in a/an — a hell of a game, one hell of a mess, one heck of an argument. Never a plural (✗ a hell of a games) and never a bare uncountable (✗ a hell of a traffic, ✗ a hell of a money). To reach the other two noun types you hang the frame on a quantifier instead: a hell of a lot of people, a hell of a lot of money. The noun itself may be good, bad, or neutral — the frame only supplies the intensity, and the direction comes from the noun.
entries.ofRule: The of is welded into the frame and cannot be dropped: ✗ a hell a game. It is not the partitive of, so no determiner may follow it (✗ a hell of the game) and no pronoun may either (✗ a hell of a them) — for a pronoun you go through the lot version, a hell of a lot of them.
entries.pattern: a/one hell of a(n) + [singular countable noun] · a/one hell of a(n) + [adjective] + [noun] · one heck of a(n) + [noun] (euphemism) · a hell of a lot of + [plural or uncountable] · the hell out of (unrelated verb intensifier)
entries.contrast: This is quite a with the volume up and the collar down — quite a game and a hell of a game fill the identical slot and make the identical claim, and only register separates them. Against such a, the word order matches (a hell of a long day, such a long day, adjective after the article), which is what keeps both of them apart from so, the one degree word that drags the adjective in front (so long a day). One hell of a is simply the emphatic form of a hell of a; the one is not counting anything, which is why ✗ two hells of a mess is nonsense. Keep the determiner apart from the adverbial the hell of what the hell and get the hell out, which intensifies verbs and question words rather than nouns. On the euphemism: heck is not merely politer but weaker — one heck of a storm is what the local news anchor says, one hell of a storm is what the man whose roof came off says.
variants: a hell of a lot of
entries.meaning: Marks the noun as an extreme instance of its kind, in either direction: a hell of a mechanic is very good and a hell of a mess is very bad, and only the noun tells you which. It is among the commonest intensifiers in spoken American English and among the rarest in edited writing — which is exactly why one heck of a exists.
examples: That was a hell of a game, right down to the last out.
He is one hell of a mechanic — nobody else could find that leak.
We got one heck of a storm out of that front Tuesday night.
Losing the server on a Friday was a hell of a way to end the week.
She has had a hell of a year, and not in a good way.
That is a helluva view for eighty dollars a night.
It would take one hell of an argument to change his mind now.
There is still a hell of a lot of work to do before the inspection.

entries.respell: uh WAYL uv uh — most Americans use a plain /w/ rather than the older /ʍ/, so whale is a homophone of wail; the weak forms are the frame's usual ones, of to /əv/ and then /ə/, both articles to /ə/ (/ən/ before a vowel), and the phrase surfaces as a single run, /ə ˈweɪləvə/, uh WAY-luh-vuh
entries.register: informal, American, and mildly dated — the clean cousin of a hell of a. An American meets it in sportscasting, in advertising copy, and from relatives over sixty, and above all in the frozen phrase have a whale of a time
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only — a whale of a time, a whale of a story, a whale of an idea. Never a plural (✗ a whale of a stories) and never a bare uncountable (✗ a whale of a fun). Unlike a hell of a it leans positive: a whale of a time is a good time, and a whale of a mess is possible but sounds like a joke. There is no a whale of a lot of in current use, so for plurals and uncountables you switch to a lot of or a great deal of.
entries.ofRule: Of is welded into the frame and cannot be dropped: ✗ a whale a time. It is not partitive, so nothing definite may follow it — ✗ a whale of the time, ✗ a whale of it. Compare the literal noun, where the of is doing real work: the skeleton of a whale.
entries.pattern: a whale of a(n) + [singular countable noun] · a whale of a(n) + [adjective] + [noun] · have a whale of a time (fixed collocation) · a monster/beast/bear of a + [noun] (the same frame, other animals)
entries.contrast: A whale of a and a hell of a are one construction with a different noun dropped into the frame, and they split on register and direction: the whale is clean, folksy, and usually complimentary, the hell is profane, current, and can go either way. Against quite a, the whale is louder and warmer — quite a time is what you write, a whale of a time is what your grandmother says. The frame stays productive in casual speech with any noun of size (a monster of a truck, a beast of a hill, a bear of a man), and those obey the same rules; what earns a whale of a its own entry is that it has frozen into have a whale of a time, where no other animal will substitute. It has nothing to do with the literal noun whale, and nothing at all to do with the verb wail.
variants: have a whale of a time (fixed)
a hell of a (the profane equivalent)
entries.meaning: An intensifier meaning "a very big and usually very good one of these," built on the size of the animal. It is the mildest member of the a … of a family and the one member you can use in front of anybody's children.
examples: The kids had a whale of a time at the lake.
That was a whale of a story, and I do not believe a word of it.
We ran into a whale of a problem with the foundation.
She has a whale of an argument for keeping the old building.
They threw a whale of a party when he finally retired.
It turned out to be a whale of a deal once they threw in the warranty.
He hit a whale of a home run to end the game in the ninth.
related: a hell of a, one hell of a, one heck of a

entries.respell: awl BUT — but keeps its full vowel here, unlike the conjunction, which reduces to /bət/
entries.register: neutral, slightly formal
entries.goesWith: whatever all itself goes with, since it is all with an exception clipped on. Plural countable nouns (all but two passengers), uncountable nouns (all but a cup of the flour, all but a trickle of the water), and singular countable nouns only when a determiner follows (all but the final chapter). Never a bare singular countable: ✗ all but chapter. The exception phrase after but must be a noun phrase, a numeral, or a pronoun. Agreement: the verb follows the plural set, not the singular exception standing next to it — All but one of the founders have retired, never ✗ has retired. With an uncountable noun the verb is singular: All but a trickle of the water was gone.
entries.ofRule: Of attaches to the exception, not to all. It is required before a pronoun — all but two of them, all but one of us, never ✗ all but two them. With a following determiner it is optional in the same way as bare all: all but (a few) of the seats.
entries.pattern: all but + [the/my/this + noun] · all but + [numeral] + [plural noun] · all but + [numeral] + of + [the/them] · all but one · all but + [adjective/verb] (the unrelated adverb)
entries.contrast: As a determiner all but means "every one except," and the exception is a real countable thing you could point to. As an adverb it means "almost" and modifies an adjective or a verb: the project was all but finished does not mean everything except the finishing. The test is what follows — a noun phrase means determiner, an adjective or participle means adverb. Against most, all but claims far more: most of the seats leaves the count vague, while all but three of the seats names exactly what is missing. Against not all, it points the other way: not all of the seats sold says some did not, all but three of the seats sold says almost every one did. Determiner or pronoun: both. With the noun spelled out it is a determiner (all but three passengers); with the noun understood from context the phrase stands alone as a pronoun (Twelve boarded, and all but three walked away), and the pronoun use keeps the plural verb.
entries.meaning: Sweeps in the entire set and then carves out a named exception, which is why it feels more precise than most — the speaker is telling you exactly how much is left over.
examples: All but three of the passengers walked away from the crash.
She has read all but the last chapter.
All but one of the original founders have retired.
The storm knocked out power to all but a handful of houses on the street.
All but two of them voted to postpone the decision.
They sold off all but the downtown property.
We used all but a cup of the flour on the first batch.
Has all but the last shipment cleared customs yet?
Twelve people boarded, and all but three walked away.

entries.respell: KWYTE-uh — often flapped to /ˈkwaɪɾə/ in fast speech; before a vowel the article takes its weak an /ən/, as in quite an evening /ˌkwaɪt ən ˈivnɪŋ/
entries.register: neutral and conversational
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only in this predeterminer use — quite a while, quite a mess, quite an evening. Never a plural (✗ quite a friends) and never a bare uncountable (✗ quite a traffic, ✗ quite a money). To reach the other two noun types you switch phrases: plural countable takes quite a few (quite a few neighbors), and uncountable takes quite a bit of (quite a bit of money) or article-free quite some (quite some time, quite some trouble).
entries.ofRule: No of on quite a itself — ✗ quite a of the time. The repair phrases do take it: quite a few of them, quite a bit of the money. Quite some takes none: ✗ quite some of time.
entries.pattern: quite a(n) [singular countable noun] · quite a(n) [adjective] + [singular countable noun] · quite the [singular countable noun] · quite a few [plural countable] · quite a bit of [uncountable] · quite some [uncountable]
entries.contrast: quite a and rather a fill the identical slot with opposite attitudes — quite a is admiring and impressed, rather a is understated and mildly negative. American English uses quite a constantly and rather a almost never. Note also the transatlantic trap in bare quite + adjective: American quite good means "very good," while British quite good often means "fairly good, and not much more." Word order matters too — quite a long while is right and ✗ a quite long while is not, because the adjective belongs after the article, not after quite. In the negative the word flips sense entirely: not quite a year means "almost a year, and slightly short of it," the opposite of the intensifying quite a year. Negate the sentence and you get the intensifier back (That wasn't quite a disaster = almost one); negate nothing and quite a only ever exaggerates.
variants: quite some (as in quite some time)
entries.meaning: 1. As an intensifier, marks the noun as a notable, impressive, or extreme instance of its kind — that was quite a storm means the storm was remarkable. 2. With measure nouns it simply means "a considerable amount of" — quite a while, quite a distance, quite a drive.
examples: That was quite a game last night.
We waited quite a while before anyone came to the door.
She has made quite a name for herself in the last two years.
It is quite a drive from here — about four hours with traffic.
He is quite the storyteller once he gets going.
Quite a few of my neighbors have put solar panels on the roof.
They spent quite a bit of money getting the roof replaced.
We waited quite some time before the doors opened.
Isn't that quite an improvement over last year's numbers?
It has been not quite a year since she started — she is short by two weeks.

entries.respell: RA-thur-uh — first syllable rhymes with bath, not with father; the article stays weak and becomes /ən/ before a vowel, as in rather an ordeal /ˌræðɚ ən ɔrˈdil/
entries.register: formal and British-leaning; in American English it reads as bookish
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only — rather a nuisance, rather a shame, rather a long meeting. Never a plural (✗ rather a problems) and never a bare uncountable (✗ rather a traffic). With plurals and uncountables the phrase becomes rather a lot of: rather a lot of people, rather a lot of traffic.
entries.ofRule: No of on rather a itself. Rather a lot of carries it obligatorily: rather a lot of money, rather a lot of them.
entries.pattern: rather a(n) [singular countable noun] · rather a(n) [adjective] + [singular countable noun] · a rather [adjective] + [noun] (the preferred American order) · rather a lot of [plural/uncountable]
entries.contrast: rather a downtones and apologizes where quite a admires: that was quite a performance is praise and that was rather a disappointment is a soft complaint. The bigger practical point is word order — American English moves the word into the ordinary adverb slot and says a rather long meeting, while rather a long meeting is the British-leaning predeterminer order. Both are grammatical; only one sounds American. Note that when rather means "instead" (I'd rather walk) it is not a determiner at all.
entries.meaning: Marks the noun as more so than expected, in a mild and faintly negative direction — the sense of "somewhat of a" or "a bit of a." The understatement is the point: rather a problem is a real problem being described politely.
examples: The whole business turned into rather a nuisance.
It was rather a shame the concert got rained out.
Losing the file that late in the day was rather a problem.
He gave rather a long answer to a very simple question.
She struck me as rather a serious person.
That is rather a lot of money for a used bike.

entries.respell: SOH, TOO, AZ — as reduces to /əz/ when unstressed, too never does
entries.register: neutral to formal; the construction is written rather than spoken
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only, because the pattern is built around a/an — so long a day, too big a risk, as good a time as any. Never a plural (✗ too big a risks, ✗ too big risks) and never an uncountable (✗ too heavy a traffic). With plurals and uncountables the pattern is simply unavailable: you rephrase (days that are so long) or switch to the ordinary quantifiers so many, too much, and as many, which take no article at all.
entries.ofRule: No of. The tails these words take are correlative, not partitive — as ... as (as good a time as any) and too ... to (too big a risk to take).
entries.pattern: so + [adjective] + a(n) + [singular noun] · too + [adjective] + a(n) + [singular noun] (+ to + verb) · as + [adjective] + a(n) + [singular noun] + as [X] · how + [adjective] + a(n) + [singular noun] (interrogative) · that + [adjective] + a(n) + [singular noun] (informal)
entries.contrast: This is the one construction in English where the adjective jumps in front of the article. Ordinary order is a long day; add one of these degree words and it inverts to so long a day — never ✗ a so long day. Compare such, which is a predeterminer in its own right and leaves the adjective where it was: such a long day. That is why such a is the everyday choice and so long a day reads as literary. Keep this pattern apart from so many, too much, and as many, which are ordinary quantifiers of plural and uncountable nouns with no article and no inversion.
entries.meaning: Marks the degree of an adjective when the noun phrase is a singular countable, and pays for it by dragging the adjective in front of a/an. In current American English this is a written construction; in speech people nearly always reach for such a or a relative clause instead.
examples: I had never seen so large a crowd at a school board meeting.
It was too big a risk to take with someone else's money.
This is as good a time as any to tell her.
How serious a problem are we actually talking about?
He is not so young a man that he can afford to wait another year.
That is too fine a distinction for a jury to follow.
Is it really that big a deal if we go on Sunday instead?

entries.respell: SUM-thing uv uh — weak forms run deep here: of goes to /əv/ and then to bare /ə/, the article is /ə/ (/ən/ before a vowel), and something itself reduces to /ˈsʌmpm̩/ in ordinary fast speech, so the whole phrase can land as /ˈsʌmpm̩ əvə/, SUMP-m-uh-vuh. Only the first syllable ever carries stress
entries.register: neutral and literate — the natural register of profiles, reviews, and obituaries, and the American print equivalent of British rather a
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only, and overwhelmingly nouns of role, type, or reputation — something of a legend, something of a specialist, something of a disaster. Never a plural (✗ something of a legends) and never a bare uncountable (✗ something of a trouble). The noun has to be one that a person or thing can be: ✓ something of an expert, and something of a chair is not English. For quantity rather than category the frame changes shape entirely — something like forty people, a certain amount of luck.
entries.ofRule: Of is built into the frame and cannot be dropped: ✗ something a legend. It is not partitive, so no determiner may follow it: ✗ something of the legend. Keep it apart from the free partitive something of meaning "a portion of," which takes no article after it and is a different construction: He has something of his father in him.
entries.pattern: [subject] + be/become + something of a(n) + [singular countable noun] · something of a(n) + [adjective] + [noun] · something like + [numeral] (approximation, unrelated) · quite something (predicative, unrelated)
entries.contrast: Where a hell of a exaggerates, something of a hedges — she is something of an expert claims deliberately less than she is an expert, which makes it the exact opposite number of quite a, a frame that claims more than the plain noun would. It is closest in tone to rather a, but not in geography: rather a nuisance is British-leaning and bookish, while something of a nuisance is what an American newspaper prints for the same idea. Against a certain, note what each one withholds — a certain charm withholds the identity of the thing, something of a charmer withholds the degree. The disputed sibling is somewhat of a, which many editors treat as an error for something of a; it is common in American speech and still worth avoiding on paper. The informal spoken equivalent is a bit of a (a bit of a mess).
entries.meaning: Hedges the noun: the thing counts as a member of the category, but only loosely, and the speaker wants credit for the qualification. That built-in reservation is why obituaries and profiles lean on it so hard — something of a recluse is the polite way to report the fact.
examples: She is something of a legend in the county clerk's office.
The evening turned into something of a disaster once the power went out.
He has become something of an expert on rural broadband.
The ruling came as something of a surprise to everyone in the room.
The old mill is something of a landmark, though nobody has worked there since 1978.
Her second novel was something of a departure from the first.
He was something of a recluse in his last years.
That is something of an overstatement, if you look at the actual numbers.
related: a hell of a, one hell of a, one heck of a

entries.respell: such-un-SUCH — the middle word is and in its weak form only, /ən/ or syllabic /n̩/, never the full /ænd/, which is why the spelling looks longer than the word sounds. The article behind it weakens too, to /ə/ or /ən/, so such-and-such a date is /ˌsʌtʃ ən ˌsʌtʃ ə ˈdeɪt/ and such-and-such an amount is /ˌsʌtʃ ən ˌsʌtʃ ən əˈmaʊnt/
entries.position: predeterminer before a/an; central determiner in the looser bare-noun use
entries.register: neutral and spoken, faintly impatient. An American meets it wherever someone is walking a listener through a procedure whose real values do not matter yet — a teacher setting up a word problem, a lawyer explaining a filing deadline, a customer-service script
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns through the article — such-and-such a date, such-and-such an amount, on such-and-such a day. It can also attach straight to a plural countable (such-and-such chapters) or an uncountable (such-and-such information) with nothing in front, though that bare use is much rarer and reads as looser speech; the article version is the standard one. It never follows an article itself: ✗ a such-and-such day, ✗ the such-and-such date. And it takes no adjective between itself and the noun in the bare use: such-and-such a long delay is fine, ✗ such-and-such long delays is not.
entries.ofRule: No of — ✗ such-and-such of the dates. To select from a set that really exists, switch to whichever or the formal certain of.
entries.pattern: such-and-such a(n) + [singular countable] · such-and-such + [plural or uncountable noun] (looser) · on/at/by such-and-such a + [time noun] · such-and-such standing alone (pronoun) · so-and-so (the person equivalent)
entries.contrast: Such-and-such is the placeholder to such's real demonstrative: such a day points at a day that actually happened, while such-and-such a day is an empty slot waiting for a date nobody has supplied. Its siblings divide the territory — so-and-so stands in for a person (talk to so-and-so in accounting) and doubles as a mild insult (the old so-and-so); thingamajig and whatchamacallit stand in for an object whose name has escaped the speaker; blah blah blah stands in for the content of what was said. Against a certain, the difference is who is being kept in the dark: a certain date means the speaker knows it and will not say, such-and-such a date means nobody has picked one. Determiner or pronoun: both. In front of a noun it is a determiner (such-and-such a form); with the noun understood it stands alone as a pronoun (he claimed he had done such-and-such), exactly as so-and-so does. Hyphens are standard in edited writing; the open spelling such and such is common and is not an error.
entries.meaning: A deliberate blank. The speaker names the slot instead of the value, either because the value is beside the point of the example or because it has not been decided yet — you file by such-and-such a date, and if you miss it the clerk does such-and-such.
examples: You have to file the form by such-and-such a date or the case is dismissed.
The letter always says the same thing: the account was reviewed on such-and-such a day and closed.
Suppose the contractor bills you for such-and-such an amount and you dispute it.
He kept saying he had been at such-and-such a meeting with so-and-so from the mayor's office.
Every syllabus tells you to read such-and-such chapters by Friday and says nothing about how.
The form just asks you to enter such-and-such information and press submit.
Do not tell me you were held up by such-and-such — I want the actual reason.

entries.respell: in-TYRE — the word begins with a vowel, so the article in front of it takes its pre-vowel forms: the entire day /ði ɪnˈtaɪɚ ˈdeɪ/, an entire block /ən ɪnˈtaɪɚ ˈblɑk/
entries.register: neutral, emphatic
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns (an entire day, the entire team), uncountable nouns naming a bounded span or mass (the entire time, the entire output), and plural countables when the plural names a fixed collection (my entire savings, the entire proceeds). It cannot open a noun phrase by itself: ✗ Entire building burned down. There must be a central determiner in front of it.
entries.ofRule: No of — ✗ the entire of the day. This is the sharpest difference from its synonym whole, where the whole of the day is fine. The of-form belongs to the noun entirety: the entirety of the day.
entries.pattern: [the/a/an/my/this] + entire + [noun] · [the] + entire + [ordinal or numeral] + [noun] · the entirety of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: entire and whole occupy the same slot and mean the same thing, but whole is the everyday word and entire the emphatic, slightly more formal one. Two grammatical splits separate them: whole takes an of-phrase and entire does not, and whole has the informal infixed form a whole nother which entire lacks. Against all, the difference is purely positional — all is a predeterminer and comes before the article (all the cake), while entire is a postdeterminer and comes after it (the entire cake), which is why ✗ the all cake and ✗ entire the cake are both impossible.
entries.meaning: The whole of something with nothing left out, said with emphasis. The speaker is not merely reporting the extent but insisting that it really was total.
examples: He spent the entire afternoon on hold with the airline.
The fire took out an entire block of downtown.
She read the entire contract before signing anything.
My entire family showed up — all fourteen of them.
He was on his phone the entire time we were at dinner.
The entire proceeds from the sale go to the food bank.

entries.respell: EK-struh — vowel-initial, so the determiner in front weakens to /ən/ or /ði/: an extra key /ən ˈɛkstrə ˈki/, the extra time /ði ˈɛkstrə ˈtaɪm/
entries.register: neutral and everyday
entries.goesWith: all three noun types, which makes it unusually flexible — singular countable (an extra key), plural countable (three extra chairs, extra towels), and uncountable (extra time, extra money, extra sugar). With a plural or an uncountable it can also open the phrase with no central determiner at all: Extra chairs are in the closet. With a singular countable it needs one: ✗ Extra key is under the mat.
entries.ofRule: No of — ✗ extra of the chairs. To quantify from a known set, use another, more of, or a numeral: two more of the chairs.
entries.pattern: [a/an/the/my] + extra + [singular noun] · [numeral] + extra + [plural noun] · extra + [plural or uncountable noun] · a little extra [uncountable]
entries.contrast: extra and additional fill the same slot and mean nearly the same thing; extra is the plain spoken word and additional the formal written one, and extra carries a hint of "spare, beyond what was strictly needed" that additional lacks. Against more, note that more is comparative and can stand alone as a pronoun (I want more) while extra as a determiner needs its noun. Do not confuse the determiner with the adverb extra meaning "unusually" (extra careful, extra spicy), which modifies adjectives rather than nouns.
entries.meaning: Beyond the number or amount already counted on — one more, or some more, added to a baseline that both speaker and listener already have in mind.
examples: Bring an extra charger in case mine dies on the road.
We put two extra chairs at the end of the table.
She stayed an extra night in Denver to finish the audit.
There is extra cash in the glove compartment.
The extra time helped, but we still missed the deadline.
Grab extra napkins on your way out.

entries.respell: OHN-lee — vowel-initial, so the in front of it is /ði/, not /ðə/: the only exit /ði ˈoʊnli ˈɛɡzɪt/
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns (the only door), plural countable nouns (the only two seats left), and uncountable nouns (the only advice she gave me, the only evidence). But it comes with a requirement the other postdeterminers do not have: it needs a definite central determiner in front of it — the, a possessive, or a demonstrative. Never after a/an (✗ an only chance), the single exception being the fixed noun an only child. Never bare: ✗ Only exit is locked.
entries.ofRule: No of on the determiner itself. The of in the only one of them belongs to one, not to only.
entries.pattern: [the/my/his/this] + only + [noun] · the only + [numeral] + [plural noun] · the only + [noun] + [relative clause] · an only child (fixed)
entries.contrast: The determiner only sits after a definite determiner and means "sole"; the far commoner adverb only sits in front of whatever it modifies and means "no more than." The slot is the test, and it changes the meaning completely: the only three people who came were her cousins identifies a group of three and says nobody else was there, while only three people came is a bare count and makes no claim about who they were. Against sole, the two words mean the same thing and differ only in register — sole is legal and written, only is what people say. In the negative it stays a determiner and simply denies uniqueness: she is not my only sister means there are others.
entries.meaning: Marks the noun as the single member of its class in the situation at hand: there are no others, and that absence is the point of the sentence.
examples: That is the only exit on this side of the building.
She is my only sister.
The only two seats left were in the back row.
His only regret was not calling sooner.
That was the only advice anyone gave me all week.
He is an only child, and it shows.
She is not my only sister — there are three of us.
Is this the only copy of the lease you have?

entries.respell: pur-TIK-yuh-lur — in fast American speech the medial schwa drops and both r's stay: /pɚˈtɪkjlɚ/, pur-TIK-lur
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns above all (a particular restaurant, this particular case, no particular reason), and uncountable nouns after no or any (no particular order, no particular hurry). Plural countables work only under these/those/no (no particular reasons, these particular files). The requirement that defines it: there must be a determiner in front — a, no, any, this, that, or the. Bare ✗ particular people objected is not the determiner use, and particular people on its own reads as the unrelated adjective meaning "fussy."
entries.ofRule: No of on the determiner. The fixed adverbial in particular (nobody in particular, in particular, the second draft) is a prepositional phrase, not a determiner.
entries.pattern: a particular + [singular countable] · no particular + [noun] · this/that particular + [singular countable] · any particular + [singular countable] · in particular (fixed adverbial)
entries.contrast: Particular and certain both narrow a noun to a specific instance, and they split on what they do with the identity. A certain restaurant means the speaker knows which one and is not telling; a particular restaurant means one specific one, with no implication of concealment. Particular also runs freely under no and this, where certain cannot: no particular reason is idiomatic and ✗ no certain reason is not. Keep the determiner apart from the adjective particular meaning "fussy, hard to please," which goes after be: she is very particular about her coffee.
entries.meaning: Narrows the noun to one specific instance rather than the general class. Under no it does the opposite job and cancels the narrowing — no particular reason means the reason was not any specific one.
examples: I had a particular restaurant in mind when I suggested dinner.
She left for no particular reason that anyone could name.
This particular case is the one the court will hear first.
Put the files back in no particular order.
Is there any particular reason you are asking me this now?
That particular model was recalled two years ago.
These particular files were never backed up.
He named no particular names, but everyone knew who he meant.

entries.respell: PAST
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: singular and plural countable nouns that name a stretch of time or a recurring event — the past week, the past three elections, these past few months. It does not take ordinary object nouns (✗ the past chair) and does not count uncountables (✗ the past water). One separate use escapes the determiner slot: generic attributive past before an abstract noun with no article at all — past experience, past performance, past behavior.
entries.ofRule: No of — ✗ the past of three weeks. The noun the past is a different thing (in the past, a thing of the past).
entries.pattern: the past + [numeral or quantifier] + [plural time noun] · the past + [singular time noun] · these/this past + [time noun] · past + [abstract noun] (generic, no article)
entries.contrast: past and last both count backward from now, and in the plural they are interchangeable: the past three weeks and the last three weeks say the same thing. The difference appears in the singular and with the article. The past year means the twelve months just ended, while last year with no the means the previous calendar year — two different spans. And last carries a second sense that past never has, "final in a series" (the last chapter), so the past chapter is not English.
entries.meaning: Counts a span backward from the present moment, covering the period that runs right up to now rather than a period that ended and closed.
examples: The past three weeks have been a blur.
Sales are up eleven percent over the past year.
She has been in and out of the hospital these past few months.
This past weekend was the first sunny one all spring.
In the past decade the neighborhood has changed completely.
Past performance is no guarantee of future results.

entries.respell: rih-SPEK-tiv
entries.register: formal and written — business, legal, and academic prose
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns only — their respective fields, the respective departments, our respective shares. Never a singular (✗ his respective office) and never an uncountable (✗ their respective luggage), because the word's entire job is to hand out one item to each of several possessors, which requires more than one of each. It also needs a determiner in front of it, almost always a possessive: ✗ Respective owners were notified.
entries.ofRule: No of — ✗ the respective of the totals.
entries.pattern: [their/our/your/the] + respective + [plural noun] · [plural subject] + verb + to their respective + [plural noun] · [list] + respectively (adverb)
entries.contrast: respective distributes where same collects. They went back to their respective offices means each person went to a different office, one apiece; They went back to the same office means one office for everybody. Against own, which also follows a possessive, own stresses ownership against an outsider (her own car) while respective stresses the one-to-one matching inside a group. Do not confuse it with respectful ("showing respect"), an unrelated adjective.
entries.meaning: Assigns one item to each member of a plural set — "each one's own," matched up one to one, with the matching itself being the information the word contributes.
examples: After the meeting everyone went back to their respective desks.
The two companies kept their respective logos after the merger.
Both authors are leaders in their respective fields.
The delegates flew home to their respective countries on Sunday.
Please list the respective totals for each quarter.
My brother and I inherited our respective shares of the house.

entries.respell: SELF-same
entries.register: literary and emphatic — rare in speech, a written flourish
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns overwhelmingly (the selfsame moment, the selfsame bench), occasionally plural countables (the selfsame words), and uncountable abstract nouns in stretched literary use (that selfsame stubbornness). It requires the or a demonstrative in front of it — never a/an (✗ a selfsame day), because asserting identity presupposes a referent the reader can already find. Never bare: ✗ Selfsame bench sat there for years.
entries.ofRule: No of.
entries.pattern: [the/this/that] + selfsame + [noun] · the very selfsame + [noun] (double emphasis) · that selfsame + [time noun]
entries.contrast: This is same with the volume turned up. The same day is neutral reporting; the selfsame day insists on the coincidence and asks the reader to be struck by it. Very does a similar emphatic job (that very day), and the two stack into that very selfsame day. In ordinary American English the very same is the natural phrase and selfsame the deliberately bookish one — use it in fiction, not in a memo.
variants: the very same (the plain modern equivalent)
entries.meaning: Marks two things as not merely alike but numerically one and the same, with the writer stressing how remarkable the coincidence is.
examples: They met again on the selfsame bench thirty years later.
That selfsame argument had already cost him one job.
She wore the selfsame dress to both weddings.
At that selfsame moment the power went out across the city.
He repeated the selfsame words his father had used on him.
The letter arrived on the selfsame day she decided to leave.

entries.respell: SOHL — a homophone of soul and of sole the fish
entries.register: formal and written — legal, journalistic, and business prose; in speech Americans say only
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns (the sole heir, the sole survivor) and uncountable abstract nouns (its sole purpose, sole responsibility). Plural countables are possible but stilted (the sole survivors), where only is the natural choice. It normally needs the or a possessive in front of it — ✗ a sole survivor — with one systematic exception: fixed legal collocations take the zero article before an uncountable, as in sole custody, sole discretion, and sole ownership.
entries.ofRule: No of on the determiner. The of in the sole author of the report belongs to author, not to sole.
entries.pattern: [the/my/its/our] + sole + [noun] · the sole + [noun] + of + [phrase] · sole custody / sole discretion / sole proprietor (fixed, no article)
entries.contrast: sole and only are one idea in two registers — the sole survivor is what the newspaper prints and the only survivor is what people say. Sole is more absolute and legalistic, and it locks into fixed phrases where only would be wrong: ✗ only custody, ✗ at our only discretion. Do not confuse it with the unrelated nouns sole (bottom of a foot or shoe) and sole (a flatfish), nor with solely, the adverb.
entries.meaning: The one and only — chosen over only when the exclusivity is the legally or factually load-bearing point of the sentence.
examples: She was the sole survivor of the crash.
The company's sole purpose is to license the patent.
He was named sole executor of the estate.
Refunds are issued at our sole discretion.
Their sole source of income is the rent from the garage.
She has sole custody of both children.

entries.respell: VEH-ree
entries.register: neutral, emphatic
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns above all (the very moment, this very room), plural countable nouns when they form a fixed set (his very words, the very people who complained), and uncountable abstract nouns (the very existence of the program). It requires a definite central determiner — the, a demonstrative, or a possessive — and never follows a/an in this use: ✗ a very house meaning "exactly that house."
entries.ofRule: No of.
entries.pattern: [the/this/that/my] + very + [noun] · the very + [ordinal or superlative] + [noun] · the very same + [noun] · the very + [noun] + [relative clause]
entries.contrast: This determiner very is a different word from the adverb very, which intensifies adjectives and adverbs (very tired, very quickly). What follows tells them apart: a noun means determiner (the very house), an adjective means adverb (a very old house). Against same, the two stack in the very same day but differ alone — very means "exactly this one and no other," while same means "identical to the one already mentioned."
entries.meaning: 1. Marks the noun as exactly the one in question and no other, usually with a note of surprise, irony, or emphasis. 2. With edge nouns and superlatives it marks the extreme limit — the very top, the very end, the very first.
examples: That is the very thing I was looking for.
We are standing in the very room where the treaty was signed.
He used my very words against me in the meeting.
She quit on the very day her bonus vested.
The very idea of moving again exhausts her.
Their names were at the very bottom of the list.
Come here this very minute.
The very existence of the program is now in question.
Those were his very words, and I wrote them down.

entries.respell: HOHL — the w is silent; a homophone of hole
entries.register: neutral — the everyday word for totality
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns (a whole pizza, the whole team) and uncountable nouns (the whole truth, my whole attention). With a numeral it can also front a plural time expression treated as one block: the whole three days, the whole ten dollars. Bare plurals belong to a different, adjectival sense meaning "intact, not cut up" — whole grains, whole peppercorns. It cannot open a phrase with a singular countable: ✗ Whole cake was gone.
entries.ofRule: Optional and structural. The whole summer and the whole of the summer are both good, and the of-version needs a determiner after it in American usage — the whole of the summer, where bare the whole of summer reads as British. Before a pronoun of is required: the whole of it, never ✗ the whole it.
entries.pattern: [the/a/my/this] + whole + [noun] · [the] + whole + [numeral] + [plural noun] · the whole of + [the/my + noun] · the whole of it · a whole nother (nonstandard)
entries.contrast: whole and entire mean the same and sit in the same slot, but only whole takes an of-phrase, and whole is the plain word where entire is the emphatic one. The slot is what separates whole from all: all is a predeterminer and goes before the central determiner (all the cake), whole is a postdeterminer and goes after it (the whole cake) — hence ✗ whole the cake and ✗ the all cake. With a plural noun all is the only option: all the students, never ✗ the whole students.
variants: a whole lot of (informal, large quantity)
entries.meaning: The complete extent of something with nothing missing — the same idea as all, differing only in which slot it occupies. Note the widespread spoken form a whole nother, which splits another around whole; it is nonstandard in writing and very common in American speech, but the written form is a whole other. For whole as the totality member of the fractions family, see the whole (of).
examples: He ate a whole pizza by himself.
She told me the whole story on the drive home.
I have lived in this town my whole life.
The whole team showed up to help him move.
It rained the whole three days we were there.
We spent the whole of the summer painting the house.
That is a whole other problem, and we will get to it later.

entries.term: all kinds of, all sorts of
entries.respell: awl KYNDZ uv, awl SORTS uv — of reduces to /əv/ or just /ə/
entries.register: informal to neutral, heavily spoken
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns (all kinds of birds, all sorts of problems) and uncountable nouns (all kinds of trouble, all sorts of advice). Never a singular countable: ✗ all kinds of book, ✗ all sorts of mistake. The phrase occupies the whole central slot, so no article may follow it and none may precede it.
entries.ofRule: Of is built into the phrase and cannot be dropped: ✗ all kinds problems. It is not the partitive of, so no determiner may follow it: ✗ all kinds of the problems. To select from a known set, switch to all of the problems.
entries.pattern: all kinds of [plural countable] · all kinds of [uncountable] · all sorts of [plural or uncountable] · all kinds of [adjective] + [plural noun]
entries.contrast: Read literally the phrase says "every variety of," but in ordinary American use it has drifted to mean simply "a lot of, and varied" — we had all kinds of trouble means plenty of trouble, not trouble of every possible type. All sorts of is identical in meaning and marginally more British-sounding; all manner of is the formal cousin. Against what kind of, which asks a question about type, this phrase asserts quantity and gives up on type.
entries.meaning: A large and varied quantity — "many, and of many different kinds," with the variety usually mattering less to the speaker than the sheer amount.
examples: There were all kinds of birds at the feeder this morning.
We ran into all sorts of problems with the building permit.
He gave me all kinds of advice I had not asked for.
The store sells all kinds of used camera gear.
She has had all sorts of trouble with that car since she bought it.
All kinds of people showed up, from students to retirees.

entries.respell: awl MAN-ur uv
entries.register: formal and literary — the written cousin of all kinds of
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns (all manner of excuses) and uncountable nouns (all manner of mischief). Never a singular countable: ✗ all manner of excuse. Note the fossilized singular inside the phrase — manner never pluralizes here: ✗ all manners of things, even though manners is a perfectly good noun meaning "polite behavior."
entries.ofRule: Of is part of the phrase and obligatory. No determiner may follow it: ✗ all manner of the excuses.
entries.pattern: all manner of [plural countable] · all manner of [uncountable] · all manner of [adjective] + [noun]
entries.contrast: Same meaning as all kinds of and all sorts of, one register higher — it belongs in essays and reportage rather than conversation. The fossilized singular is the error to watch: all manner of things is right and ✗ all manners of things is not. Compare the archaic bare manner of that survives only in what manner of man.
variants: manner of (archaic, as in what manner of man)
entries.meaning: Every variety of — a formal or literary way of saying "a great many different kinds of," typically used when the writer wants the list to feel exhaustingly long.
examples: The attic was full of all manner of forgotten junk.
He offered all manner of excuses and none of them held up.
The treaty was later blamed for all manner of troubles.
She keeps all manner of strange ingredients in the pantry.
The report catalogs all manner of accounting irregularities.
Children get into all manner of mischief on a rainy afternoon.
related: all kinds of, all sorts of

entries.respell: uh-SOR-tid
entries.position: central determiner, or postdeterminer after one
entries.register: neutral; standard on packaging and in commercial writing
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns almost exclusively — assorted cookies, assorted sizes, assorted complaints. Uncountables work only when the noun already names a collection (assorted hardware). A singular countable is impossible: ✗ an assorted cookie. It can open the phrase alone (assorted chocolates) or follow a central determiner (the assorted cables in the drawer, his assorted grievances).
entries.ofRule: No of — ✗ assorted of the cookies. The of-construction belongs to the noun: an assortment of cookies.
entries.pattern: assorted + [plural countable] · [the/his/these] + assorted + [plural countable] · assorted + [adjective] + [plural noun] · an assortment of + [plural or uncountable]
entries.contrast: Assorted and various both mean "of several different kinds," but assorted implies a mixture put together on purpose — a box of assorted chocolates was assembled by someone — while various says nothing about how the variety arose. Applied to people or problems, assorted turns faintly dismissive (assorted hangers-on). Because it takes no singular, an assortment of is the way to get an article in front.
entries.meaning: Of several different kinds mixed together, usually as a deliberate selection rather than an accident.
examples: She brought a tin of assorted cookies to the potluck.
The drawer was full of assorted cables and dead batteries.
They sell the shirts in assorted colors and sizes.
His assorted complaints about the neighbors filled two pages.
The bin held assorted screws, none of them the right length.
Assorted relatives turned up for the reading of the will.
The garage was stacked with assorted hardware he would never use.
Do they come in assorted sizes, or only the one?
related: all kinds of, all sorts of

entries.respell: SUR-tn — unstressed in the determiner use, with the article in front weakening to /ə/, as in a certain look /ə ˌsɚtn̩ ˈlʊk/; stressed only when it means "sure"
entries.position: postdeterminer after a/an; central determiner before plurals and uncountables
entries.register: neutral, slightly formal, often faintly coy
entries.goesWith: all three noun types, but each through a different door. Singular countable nouns take it only with a/an in front — a certain restaurant, a certain look, a certain Mr. Alvarez; never bare, so ✗ certain man came to the door. Plural countable nouns (certain questions, certain people) and uncountable nouns (certain evidence, certain information) take it with nothing in front at all — the word is the central determiner there, and ✗ a certain people and ✗ a certain information are both wrong. The one crossing case is a certain + abstract uncountable noun (a certain charm, a certain restlessness, a certain menace), where the article does not make the noun countable but hedges the quality; that is sense 3 of the meaning, and it is the only place a and an uncountable noun meet in this entry. It does not follow the in any of these senses; the certain answer can only mean "the sure answer."
entries.ofRule: Mostly none: certain people, never ✗ certain of people. But formal writing does allow certain of before another determiner — certain of the members objected — a bookish partitive that many editors avoid in favor of some of or several of.
entries.pattern: a certain + [singular countable] · certain + [plural countable] · certain + [uncountable] · a certain + [proper name] · certain of + [the/my + plural noun] (formal) · a certain amount of + [uncountable]
entries.contrast: The determiner certain is unstressed and means "particular, and I am not naming which"; the adjective certain is stressed and means "sure." The test is the verb be: I am certain works for the adjective, but you cannot say ✗ the people are certain meaning "the people are particular ones." Against various, certain points at specific members the speaker could name but declines to, while various only reports that there were several kinds. Against some, certain is more pointed and often insinuating: certain people should know better has an accusation in it that some people should know better softens.
entries.meaning: 1. Points at particular members of a set that the speaker knows but chooses not to name — certain people should know better. 2. Before a personal name, marks the person as unknown to the listener — a certain Dr. Reyes called. 3. In a certain + abstract noun, hedges a quality the speaker cannot quite pin down — a certain charm.
examples: Certain people should know better than to bring that up.
A certain Mr. Kowalski has been calling for you all morning.
The offer is good only under certain conditions.
There is a certain charm to the old station, run down as it is.
Certain information was withheld from the final report.
A certain amount of delay was built into the schedule.
Certain of the members objected, but the motion carried anyway.
She had a certain restaurant in mind but would not say which.
Are certain departments exempt from the freeze, or is it across the board?

entries.respell: DYE-vurz — stress on the first syllable, unlike diverse
entries.register: archaic and legal — recognize it, do not produce it
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns only — divers persons, divers occasions, divers dates. Never a singular (✗ divers person) and never an uncountable (✗ divers evidence). In its surviving legal uses it takes the central slot with nothing in front of it and no article after it; the older his divers offices pattern, with the word behind a determiner, is period English and not worth reviving.
entries.ofRule: No of.
entries.pattern: divers + [plural countable noun] · on divers occasions · divers and sundry + [plural noun]
entries.contrast: Divers and diverse are one word that split in two. Divers /ˈdaɪvɚz/ kept the old meaning "several, sundry" and first-syllable stress; diverse /dɪˈvɚs/ took the modern meaning "varied, of many kinds" and second-syllable stress. Modern writing uses diverse; divers survives almost only in indictments (on divers dates) and period prose. There is a homograph trap too: divers is spelled and pronounced exactly like the plural of diver, the person who dives, so only context tells them apart.
entries.meaning: Several, various — an archaic quantifier now confined to legal boilerplate and historical writing, where it signals age rather than adding meaning.
examples: The indictment alleged theft on divers occasions between March and July.
Divers witnesses were called before the grand jury.
He had traveled to divers countries in the course of his work.
The estate was divided among divers cousins nobody had ever met.
Divers complaints were laid before the council that spring.
She had, on divers dates, signed for packages she never received.

entries.respell: dih-VURSS — stress on the second syllable, unlike divers
entries.position: central determiner, or postdeterminer after one
entries.register: neutral to formal; heavily used in institutional and academic prose
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns (diverse backgrounds, diverse opinions) and collective or uncountable nouns naming a body or a body of work (a diverse workforce, diverse programming). A singular countable works only when it names a collection — a diverse team is fine, ✗ a diverse book is not. It opens the phrase alone (diverse opinions) or follows a determiner (the diverse interests of the members, our diverse staff).
entries.ofRule: No of on the determiner. The construction a diverse range of puts the of on range.
entries.pattern: diverse + [plural countable] · [the/our/a] + diverse + [collective noun] · a diverse range of + [plural noun] · [subject] + be + diverse (predicative)
entries.contrast: Diverse stresses that the members differ from each other; various only reports that there were several kinds; several counts without commenting on variety at all. The grammatical tell is the predicative slot: the panel is diverse is perfectly normal, which is why diverse is usually classed as an adjective that also does determiner work, whereas ✗ the panel is various is not English. Keep it apart from archaic divers /ˈdaɪvɚz/, which means "several" and is stressed on the first syllable.
entries.meaning: Made up of members that differ markedly from one another in origin, kind, or character — the difference among them being the information the word supplies.
examples: The committee heard diverse opinions before it voted.
She works with a diverse team spread across four countries.
Diverse interests pulled the coalition apart within a year.
The catalog covers a diverse range of subjects, from beekeeping to bookbinding.
The city's population is far more diverse now than it was in 1990.
Their portfolio is deliberately diverse so that no one sector can sink it.

entries.respell: GIV-un
entries.register: neutral to formal; common in technical, statistical, and sports writing
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only — any given moment, a given category, any given Sunday. Never a plural (✗ any given days) and never an uncountable (✗ a given water), because the phrase exists to pick out exactly one arbitrary instance. It requires a or any in front of it and never follows the in this sense.
entries.ofRule: No of.
entries.pattern: any given + [singular countable] · a given + [singular countable] · at any given + [time noun] · in a given + [period or category]
entries.contrast: Any given and plain any both choose freely, but any given fixes on one arbitrary instance and then reasons about it: on any given day about forty people come through is a claim about a single representative day, while any day works for me offers the entire range at once. Do not confuse the determiner with the preposition given meaning "considering" (Given the weather, we should leave early), nor with the noun a given meaning "something taken for granted" (That's a given).
entries.meaning: Any one instance you care to pick, considered on its own as a representative stand-in for all the others.
examples: On any given day about forty people come through the clinic.
At any given moment there are roughly ten thousand planes in the air.
In a given month she will drive maybe six hundred miles.
Any given Sunday, either team could win that game.
The rule applies to all employees in a given pay grade.
Only three cases are open at any given time.

entries.respell: MAN-uh-fohld — first-syllable stress and a full /oʊ/ in the last syllable, as in twofold; the middle vowel is a schwa that can drop out entirely in fast speech, /ˈmænfoʊld/. Being a content word it has no weak form of its own — what reduces is the determiner in front of it, as in the manifold blessings /ðə ˈmænəfoʊld ˈblɛsɪŋz/ and his manifold talents /ɪz ˈmænəfoʊld ˈtælənts/
entries.position: central determiner, or postdeterminer after one
entries.register: archaic, literary, and scriptural — recognize it, and produce it only when the King James sound is what you are after
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns (manifold reasons, manifold blessings) and abstract uncountable nouns naming something that comes in kinds (manifold wisdom, manifold grace). Never a singular countable: ✗ a manifold reason. It opens the phrase with no article at all (manifold difficulties) or drops back behind a determiner (the manifold failures of the agency, his manifold talents). It also sits predicatively after be — the benefits are manifold — which is both the tell that it is an adjective doing determiner work, in the way diverse is, and its commonest surviving use in modern American writing.
entries.ofRule: No of — ✗ manifold of the reasons. The partitive goes through many of or several of. The unrelated noun a manifold (the exhaust manifold of an engine, a manifold in topology) carries its own article and its own of: the manifold of a six-cylinder engine.
entries.pattern: manifold + [plural countable] · manifold + [abstract uncountable] · [the/his/its] + manifold + [plural noun] · [subject] + be + manifold (predicative — the live modern use) · a manifold (noun, unrelated)
entries.contrast: Manifold belongs to the variety family with various, sundry, divers, and diverse, and it is the most elevated of them: various reasons is what you write, manifold reasons is what a hymn sings. Where an American actually meets it: the King James Bible (the manifold wisdom of God, Ephesians 3:10; manifold temptations, 1 Peter 1:6), the hymns and prayers built on that vocabulary, nineteenth-century prose, and the one formula that survives intact in ordinary speech and business writing, the benefits are manifold. Against myriad, which stresses sheer number, manifold stresses kinds — many, and folded over into many sorts. Against multiple, which is flat and clinical, it is warm and elevated, which is why an incident report says multiple injuries and a eulogy says his manifold kindnesses. It is built like the multipliers twofold and tenfold but does not count: ✗ sales rose manifold is not the way to say sales rose tenfold. Do not misread it as manifest, an unrelated word.
variants: a manifold (noun: engine part, mathematical object)
entries.meaning: Many and of many kinds at once — the old word for a number that is large because the varieties are. In front of a noun in ordinary modern prose it reads as deliberate period costume; after be it is still perfectly current.
examples: The committee's failures were manifold and well documented.
He thanked the congregation for its manifold kindnesses that winter.
Manifold difficulties delayed the expedition for the whole of that summer.
The King James translators wrote of the manifold wisdom of God, and the phrase has stuck.
Her manifold talents were wasted on a job that only ever asked her to file invoices.
The benefits of the merger are manifold, and the costs all sit in one column.
The old prayer book gives thanks for God's manifold mercies.
The shop had to order a new exhaust manifold, which is a different word altogether.

entries.respell: miss-uh-LAY-nee-us
entries.position: central determiner, or postdeterminer after one
entries.register: neutral to formal; the standard label on forms, budgets, and inventories
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns (miscellaneous charges, miscellaneous parts) and uncountable nouns naming an undifferentiated mass (miscellaneous debris, miscellaneous paperwork). A singular countable is odd unless it names a collection: ✗ a miscellaneous receipt. It opens the phrase alone (miscellaneous expenses) or follows a determiner (the miscellaneous items at the back of the shelf).
entries.ofRule: No of on the determiner. The noun miscellany carries it: a miscellany of odds and ends.
entries.pattern: miscellaneous + [plural countable] · miscellaneous + [uncountable] · [the] + miscellaneous + [noun] · a miscellany of + [plural noun]
entries.contrast: The variety words differ in what they imply about how the collection came to be. Assorted is a deliberate mixture; various is a neutral several-kinds; diverse stresses that the members differ; and miscellaneous is the leftover bin — things grouped only because they fit nowhere else. That is exactly why it is the standard heading for the last line of a budget and why ✗ a miscellaneous team makes no sense where a diverse team does.
entries.meaning: Of assorted kinds with no organizing principle — the catch-all category for whatever is left over after the real categories have been filled.
examples: File the receipts under miscellaneous expenses.
The box held miscellaneous parts from three different bikes.
She spent the whole afternoon on miscellaneous paperwork.
Miscellaneous charges accounted for a third of the bill.
The last drawer is for miscellaneous junk we cannot classify.
The miscellaneous items at the back of the shelf had been there for years.

entries.respell: MUL-tuh-pul — the middle syllable reduces to a schwa or drops entirely in fast speech: /ˈmʌltəpl̩/
entries.position: central determiner, or postdeterminer after one
entries.register: neutral; the default word in journalism, medical writing, and incident reports
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns only — multiple reasons, multiple witnesses, multiple times. Never a singular countable (✗ a multiple reason, ✗ multiple witness) and never an uncountable (✗ multiple advice, ✗ multiple information, ✗ multiple evidence), which is the error to watch, since the meaning tempts writers into it. For an uncountable you must go through a countable head: multiple pieces of evidence, multiple forms of aid, multiple rounds of funding. It opens the phrase alone (multiple complaints) or follows a central determiner (the multiple failures of the system, his multiple injuries). Agreement: plural verb, always — Multiple witnesses were called, never ✗ was called.
entries.ofRule: No of before a bare noun — ✗ multiple of the witnesses is not English. The partitive goes through several of or a number of: several of the witnesses. The mathematical a multiple of six is the noun multiple, a different word that carries its own of.
entries.pattern: multiple + [plural countable] · [the/his/these] + multiple + [plural countable] · multiple + [adjective] + [plural noun] · multiple + [countable head] + of + [uncountable] · a multiple of + [number] (noun, unrelated)
entries.contrast: Multiple, several, and various split three ways. Several counts loosely — more than two, fewer than many. Various adds that the members differed in kind. Multiple says only "more than one" and says it flatly, with no estimate and no flavor, which is exactly why reporting and clinical prose reach for it: multiple injuries, multiple sources, multiple offenses. It is also the one of the three that sits comfortably behind a determiner in ordinary modern prose — the multiple failures is unremarkable, while the several failures survives only in legal English, where the several means "the respective." Keep the determiner apart from the noun multiple (a multiple of twelve) and from the compound multiple-choice.
entries.meaning: More than one, stated without warmth or estimate — the plain modern word for a count the speaker wants on the record but does not want to characterize.
examples: Multiple witnesses described the same car leaving the lot.
She gave multiple reasons for leaving, and none of them was money.
The building failed multiple inspections before it was condemned.
He has been treated for multiple injuries since the accident.
The multiple failures that night were all traced to one relay.
Were there multiple offers on the house, or just the one?
The report rests on multiple pieces of evidence, not a single document.
Do not send multiple copies of the same form.

entries.respell: sum KYND uv — some takes its weak form /səm/ here and is never the stressed /sʌm/
entries.register: informal to neutral, heavily spoken
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns with their article absorbed (some kind of animal, some kind of mistake) and uncountable nouns (some kind of trouble, some kind of oil). For a plural the whole phrase pluralizes: some kinds of birds never migrate. The form some kind of a mistake, with an extra a wedged in after of, is common in casual American speech but is nonstandard in writing — drop the a.
entries.ofRule: Of is built into the phrase and cannot be dropped: ✗ some kind mistake. It is not partitive, so no determiner follows it: ✗ some kind of the animal.
entries.pattern: some kind of + [singular countable, no article] · some kind of + [uncountable] · some sort of + [noun] · some kinds of + [plural noun]
entries.contrast: Some kind of hedges the type of the thing — some kind of bird means it is a bird but I cannot say which kind. Plain some hedges its identity or amount — some bird means a bird, and I am not saying which one. The question form what kind of asks for the type instead of giving up on it. Keep the determiner apart from the adverbial hedge kind of (kind of tired, reduced to kinda), which modifies adjectives and verbs, not nouns.
variants: some kind of a (criticized in writing)
entries.meaning: Marks the noun as belonging to a category the speaker cannot or will not specify — "a something-or-other of this general type," with the vagueness openly admitted.
examples: There is some kind of animal living under the porch.
It looked like some kind of mistake on the invoice.
He is in some kind of trouble with the bank again.
They put some kind of oil on it to stop the squeaking.
She is some sort of consultant, but nobody knows for what.
Some kinds of birds never migrate at all.
Is this some kind of joke, or are you serious?
It was not some kind of accident — somebody unplugged it.
related: all kinds of, all sorts of

entries.respell: SUCH-lyke
entries.register: dated; more British than American — recognize it, do not reach for it
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns (suchlike creatures, suchlike tools) and uncountable nouns (suchlike nonsense, suchlike talk). Never a singular countable: ✗ a suchlike creature. It takes no article in front of it, and it far more often stands alone as a pronoun at the end of a list: swords, shields, and suchlike.
entries.ofRule: No of.
entries.pattern: suchlike + [plural or uncountable noun] · [list] + and suchlike (standing alone) · or suchlike
entries.contrast: Suchlike is such plus -like, and in the determiner slot it means much the same thing, "of that sort." The everyday American equivalents are that kind of and the trailing and things like that. Two differences from such matter: such is fully current in American English while suchlike is not, and such takes an article in the singular (such a day) while suchlike never does.
entries.meaning: Of that sort — used to gesture at the rest of a category rather than spell it out, usually with a touch of impatience toward the things being waved away.
examples: He had no patience for horoscopes, crystals, and suchlike nonsense.
The shed was full of rakes, hoes, and suchlike tools.
She never believed in ghosts or suchlike creatures.
They talked about mortgages, insurance, and suchlike dull matters.
Bring rope, tarps, and suchlike — whatever you would take camping.
Suchlike talk was common enough in the village at the time.
related: all kinds of, all sorts of

entries.respell: SUN-dree
entries.position: central determiner, or postdeterminer after one
entries.register: formal and dated, sometimes jocular; alive in accounting and in the fixed phrase all and sundry
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns (sundry documents, sundry relatives) and uncountable nouns naming a mass of odds and ends (sundry paperwork). Never a singular countable: ✗ a sundry document. It opens the phrase alone (sundry expenses) or follows a determiner (the sundry complaints in the file).
entries.ofRule: No of. In the fossilized phrase all and sundry the word is a pronoun meaning "everybody," not a determiner.
entries.pattern: sundry + [plural countable] · [the] + sundry + [plural noun] · all and sundry (fixed pronoun) · sundries (noun, "small miscellaneous items")
entries.contrast: Sundry, various, assorted, and miscellaneous all mean "of several kinds," and only register and flavor separate them: various is neutral and current, assorted implies a deliberate mixture, miscellaneous is the leftover bin, and sundry is the old-fashioned bookkeeper's word. It pairs with the equally archaic divers in the legal doublet divers and sundry.
entries.meaning: Various, of several sorts — a dated word for a mixed handful of small items, still standard in bookkeeping where sundry expenses is a real line on a ledger.
examples: The invoice lists sundry charges that nobody can explain.
She kept receipts, stamps, and sundry odds and ends in the top drawer.
Sundry relatives arrived over the course of the weekend.
Post the small amounts to sundry expenses.
He answered questions from reporters, neighbors, and sundry passersby.
The invitation went out to all and sundry.
There is sundry paperwork still waiting on your desk.
The auditors could not tie sundry expenses to any invoice.

entries.respell: VAIR-ee-us
entries.position: central determiner, or postdeterminer after one
entries.register: neutral — the current, unmarked member of its family
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns only — various reasons, various people, the various options. Never a singular countable (✗ a various reason) and never an uncountable (✗ various information, ✗ various advice), which is the commonest error with this word. For uncountables you must go through a countable head: various kinds of evidence, various forms of aid.
entries.ofRule: No of before a bare noun. Formal writing does allow various of before another determiner — various of the delegates walked out — but it is rare and many editors dislike it; several of the delegates is the safe alternative.
entries.pattern: various + [plural countable] · [the/its/these] + various + [plural countable] · various kinds of + [plural or uncountable] · various + [adjective] + [plural noun]
entries.contrast: Various says two things at once — there were several, and they differed. Several gives the number without the variety; diverse stresses the difference more strongly and can follow be (the group is diverse), which various barely tolerates (his reasons were various sounds literary, and ✗ the group is various is not English). Against certain, various is open about the variety and vague about which ones, while certain points at particular ones and declines to name them.
entries.meaning: Several, and of more than one kind — the ordinary modern word for a mixed handful, and the default choice whenever sundry, divers, or assorted would sound wrong.
examples: He gave various reasons for quitting, none of them convincing.
The various departments each keep their own records.
Various people have asked me the same question this week.
The drug is sold under various brand names.
She has worked in various capacities at the museum since 2011.
The report cites various kinds of evidence, most of it circumstantial.
